Author: Paperno
Title: The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context
Contribution: Introduces LAMBADA, a word prediction benchmark of 10,022 narrative passages where the last word is guessable only with broad discourse context, not the final sentence alone.
Dataset: LAMBADA; BookCorpus; Control set (5K passages from BookCorpus test novels)
Data Size: 10,022 passages (4,869 dev + 5,153 test); training corpus of 2,662 novels with 203 million words; total novel pool 5,325 books and 465 million words
Models Used: RNN (Elman); LSTM; N-Gram (SRILM); N-Gram with cache; Memory Network; Sup-CBOW; Unsup-CBOW
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy (%)=7.3 (Random capitalized word from passage LAMBADA); Perplexity=768 (N-Gram w/cache LAMBADA); Accuracy (%)=0 (LSTM LAMBADA); Accuracy (%)=21.9 (LSTM Control (5K Book Corpus passages)) | other metrics: Accuracy; Median rank of correct word
Key Results: On LAMBADA, no tested language model reaches above 1% accuracy (LSTM, RNN, Memory Network, N-Gram all 0%; N-Gram w/cache 0.1%) | LSTM accuracy: LAMBADA 0% (PPL 5357) vs Control 21.9% (PPL 149) | N-Gram with cache achieves the best LAMBADA perplexity at 768 (still 0.1% accuracy) | Random capitalized word from passage baseline reaches 7.3% accuracy on LAMBADA, beating all neural models
Strengths: Human-validated by strict crowdsourcing: each passage requires two consecutive subjects to guess the target with broad context, but no subject from a pool of ten can guess from the last sentence. | Casts long-context understanding as standard word prediction, so any language model can be tested without task-specific architecture changes. | Built from unpublished BookCorpus novels, which limits leakage of world knowledge from Wikipedia or famous books. | Establishes a wide gap between humans and 2016 language models (all under 1% accuracy), giving a clear long-term research target.
Limitations: Authors call the modelling work very preliminary and a proof-of-concept, with limited tuning of neural baselines. | Filtering selects passages where simple language models already fail, so standard LMs are bound to score near zero by design. | Strict perfect-match acceptance rule rejects synonyms or other plausible continuations, narrowing what counts as a correct answer. | Cost limited the use of more annotators at stage 1, which the authors say could improve filtering quality.

Author: Vaswani
Title: Attention Is All You Need
Contribution: Introduces the Transformer, a sequence transduction architecture based solely on self-attention, removing recurrence and convolutions and enabling far more parallel training while reaching state-of-the-art translation quality.
Dataset: WMT 2014 English-to-German; WMT 2014 English-to-French; Penn Treebank (Wall Street Journal); BerkeleyParser semi-supervised corpora (~17M sentences)
Data Size: WMT En-De ~4.5M sentence pairs (37K BPE vocab); WMT En-Fr 36M sentences (32K word-piece vocab); WSJ ~40K training sentences for parsing
Models Used: Transformer (base): N=6, d_model=512, d_ff=2048, h=8, ~65M params; Transformer (big): N=6, d_model=1024, d_ff=4096, h=16, ~213M params; Transformer (4 layers) for constituency parsing, d_model=1024
Evaluation Metrics: BLEU=28.4 (Transformer (big) WMT 2014 EN-DE (newstest2014)); BLEU=41.8 (Transformer (big) WMT 2014 EN-FR (newstest2014)); Training Cost (FLOPs)=3.3e+18 (Transformer (base) WMT 2014 EN-DE (newstest2014)); F1=91.3 (Transformer (4 layers, dmodel=1024) WSJ-23 (Penn Treebank)) | other metrics: Perplexity (per-wordpiece, dev set); WSJ section 23 F1 (constituency parsing)
Key Results: Transformer (big) reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN-DE, beating prior best (including ensembles) by over 2 BLEU | Transformer (big) reaches 41.8 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN-FR, a new single-model state of the art, after 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs | Transformer (base) reaches 27.3 BLEU EN-DE / 38.1 BLEU EN-FR at training cost 3.3×10^18 FLOPs, far below prior models | 4-layer Transformer reaches 91.3 F1 on WSJ-23 (WSJ-only) and 92.7 F1 (semi-supervised), outperforming most prior parsers
Strengths: Removes recurrence and convolutions, allowing far more parallel training and shorter wall-clock time to state of the art. | Sets a new single-model state of the art on WMT 2014 EN-DE (28.4 BLEU) and EN-FR (41.8 BLEU). | Self-attention gives O(1) maximum path length between any two positions, easing long-range dependency learning. | Generalises beyond translation: a 4-layer Transformer reaches 92.7 F1 on WSJ constituency parsing with little tuning.
Limitations: Self-attention costs O(n^2 · d) per layer, becoming expensive for very long sequences relative to recurrent layers. | Multi-head attention has reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, only partly fixed by multiple heads. | Reducing attention key size d_k hurts quality, suggesting dot-product compatibility may be insufficient. | Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting; quality also drops with too many heads.

Author: Mihaylov
Title: Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering
Contribution: OpenBookQA is a new 5,957-question multiple-choice QA benchmark paired with a 1,326-fact open book of elementary science, requiring multi-hop reasoning that combines a core fact with broad common knowledge.
Dataset: OpenBookQA (5,957 4-way multiple-choice science questions); F: 1,326 elementary science facts (open book, subset of WorldTree); K: ~6,000 auxiliary common-knowledge facts (crowdsourced second facts); ConceptNet (external knowledge source); WordNet (external knowledge source)
Data Size: 5,957 multiple-choice questions split 4,957/500/500 for Train/Dev/Test; 1,326 core science facts; ~6,000 auxiliary K facts
Models Used: PMI (Clark et al., 2016); TableILP (Khashabi et al., 2016); TupleInference (Khot et al., 2017); DGEM (Khot et al., 2018); IR solver (Clark et al., 2016); Embeddings + Similarities (logistic regression with GloVe centroids); ESIM (Chen et al., 2017b); Plausible Answer Detector (BiLSTM max-out, choice-only); Odd-One-Out Solver (BiLSTM max-out, choice-to-choices attention); Question Match (BiLSTM max-out attention); Knowledge-Enhanced Reader (variant of Mihaylov and Frank, 2018); ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) - applied to Question Match and ESIM; GloVe 300d embeddings (840B Common Crawl tokens) - input embeddings
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy=89.3 (Human OpenBookQA-Dev); Accuracy=91.7 (Human OpenBookQA-Test); Accuracy=49.6 (BiLSTM Max-Out OpenBookQA-Test); Accuracy=50.2 (BiLSTM Max-Out OpenBookQA-Test) | other metrics: accuracy (% correct on 4-way multiple choice; tie credit 1/k); standard deviation across 5 random seeds
Key Results: Human performance on OpenBookQA Test = 91.7% (Dev = 89.3%); reported as conservative Ĥ(Q)-3% lower estimate | Best knowledge-free trained baseline (Question Match / Odd-one-out) reaches 50.2% Test accuracy, far below the ~92% human level | Pre-trained science QA solvers perform near random: TupleInference 17.9%, PMI 21.2%, TableILP 23.4%, DGEM 24.4% on Test | Oracle Knowledge-Enhanced Reader given gold f and k reaches 76.9% Test, still ~15 points below human performance
Strengths: Introduces a novel open-book QA paradigm forcing multi-hop reasoning that joins one provided science fact with external common knowledge. | Multi-stage crowdsourcing plus IR/word-association adversarial filtering yields questions that defeat retrieval-only baselines. | Reports a principled human-performance estimate (~92%) using Hoeffding's inequality with high-confidence lower bounds. | Includes ablations with simplistic baselines (Plausible Answer Detector, Odd-One-Out) that expose human bias artifacts in crowdsourced QA data.
Limitations: Auxiliary fact set K is acknowledged as noisy: "often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related" to the question. | 21% of crowdsourced questions did not actually require the seed science fact, exposing a residual single-hop shortcut. | Independence assumption for human-accuracy bound is acknowledged as imperfect because the same worker may answer multiple questions. | Adding ConceptNet to the knowledge-enhanced reader hurts accuracy, indicating brittle knowledge-retrieval rather than robust reasoning.

Author: Clark
Title: BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions
Contribution: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with Wikipedia passages, used to test inferential abilities of QA models.
Dataset: BoolQ; MultiNLI; SNLI; RACE; QNLI; SQuAD 2.0; Natural Questions (NQ Long Answer); QQP (Quora Question Paraphrasing); Y/N MS Marco
Data Size: 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions: 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, 3.2k test (avg question 8.9 tokens, avg passage 108 tokens; 62.31% yes in train)
Models Used: Recurrent (BiLSTM + co-attention with fastText embeddings); Recurrent + ELMo; OpenAI GPT (12 layer, 768 dim transformer); BERT-Large (24 layer, 1024 dim)
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy (test)=80.43 (BERT-Large + MultiNLI BoolQ); Accuracy=90.0 (Human BoolQ); Accuracy (train)=62.31 (Majority BoolQ); Accuracy (test)=80.43 (BERT-Large + MultiNLI BoolQ)
Key Results: BERT-Large + MultiNLI two-step transfer reaches 80.43% test accuracy on BoolQ | Human annotators reach 90% accuracy on 110 gold-standard examples | Majority-class baseline gets 62.31% test accuracy on BoolQ | MultiNLI single-step transfer with Recurrent model reaches 75.57% on BoolQ dev (best supervised method)
Strengths: Introduces a new dataset of 16k naturally occurring yes/no questions, paired with Wikipedia passages and used as a benchmark. | Shows yes/no questions require diverse inference: less than 40% can be solved by paraphrase detection alone. | Finds MultiNLI transfer adds 3.5 points on top of BERT-Large pre-training, showing entailment data is complementary. | Releases data and code publicly to enable reproducible benchmark results.
Limitations: Uses singly-annotated examples in train, dev, and test sets to keep the dataset large. | Class imbalance: 62.31% of training answers are yes, complicating evaluation against majority baseline. | Authors note dataset has been updated since the inference analysis was done, so the type breakdown may be slightly out of date.

Author: Zellers
Title: HellaSwag: Can a Machine Really Finish Your Sentence?
Contribution: HellaSwag is a 70k-question commonsense NLI benchmark built via Adversarial Filtering (AF) with GPT generations and BERT discriminators; it is easy for humans (>95%) but hard for state-of-the-art models (<48%).
Dataset: HellaSwag; ActivityNet Captions; WikiHow; SWAG
Data Size: 70k problems total: 25k ActivityNet contexts and 45k WikiHow contexts; 10K validation and 10K test (5k in-domain + 5k zero-shot each).
Models Used: BERT-Large; BERT-Base; OpenAI GPT; ESIM+ELMo; LSTM+BERT-Base; LSTM+ELMo; LSTM+GloVe; fastText
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy=33.3 (ESIM+ELMo HellaSwag); Accuracy=47.3 (BERT-Large HellaSwag); Accuracy=45.0 (BERT-Large WikiHow); Accuracy=95.7 (Human HellaSwag) | other metrics: accuracy (%) on four-way multiple choice
Key Results: BERT-Large reaches 47.3% test accuracy on HellaSwag overall vs 95.6% human accuracy (gap > 48%) | BERT-Large drops from 86% on SWAG to 47.3% on HellaSwag, while ESIM+ELMo drops from 59% (SWAG) to 33.3% (HellaSwag) | BERT-Large zero-shot test accuracy 45.0% vs in-domain 49.7%, a 4.7-point drop on novel categories | BERT-Large transfers poorly: trained on SWAG, evaluated on HellaSwag scores only 34.6%; SWAG models on WikiHow get just 28%
Strengths: Builds a 70k commonsense NLI benchmark that is trivial for humans (>95%) yet hard for state-of-the-art models (<50%). | Identifies a Goldilocks zone of generation length where outputs fool BERT yet humans easily reject them. | Includes a zero-shot evaluation split using held-out categories to measure generalization beyond seen domains. | Releases dataset and code publicly for community use.
Limitations: Tests only models available in 2019 (BERT, GPT, ELMo); newer LLMs may quickly close the gap. | Compute extrapolation to human-level (10^9 GPU-hours) is a rough Roofline estimate, not a measurement. | Acknowledges that future models may solve HellaSwag by picking up on spurious patterns rather than reasoning.

Author: Bisk
Title: PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language
Contribution: Introduces PIQA, a multiple-choice benchmark for physical commonsense reasoning where humans reach 95% but large pretrained models (GPT, BERT, RoBERTa) plateau near 77%.
Dataset: PIQA
Data Size: Over 16,000 training QA pairs, ~2K development, ~3K test; goals average 7.8 words, solutions average 21.3 words; >3.7M lexical tokens in training
Models Used: OpenAI GPT (124M); Google BERT-Large (340M); FAIR RoBERTa-Large (355M)
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy=79.2 (RoBERTa-Large PIQA); Accuracy=77.1 (RoBERTa-Large PIQA (test)); Accuracy=94.9 (Human PIQA); Accuracy=95.0 (Human PIQA) | other metrics: Accuracy (%)
Key Results: RoBERTa-Large reaches 79.2% validation / 77.1% test accuracy on PIQA, the best of the three pretrained models | Human performance reaches 94.9% validation accuracy, ~18 points above RoBERTa | BERT-Large reaches 67.1% validation / 66.8% test, GPT 70.9% / 69.2% on PIQA | Roughly 20-point absolute gap between best model and human performance on PIQA
Strengths: Targets reporting bias by using instructables.com to seed annotators with atypical everyday tasks, flattening the object distribution. | Applies AFLite to remove stylistic artifacts that artificially inflate model accuracy on prior NLI benchmarks. | Provides a detailed error analysis showing RoBERTa fails on relations like before, after, top, bottom near chance level. | Establishes a clear ~20-point human-model gap, giving the field a measurable target for physical commonsense progress.
Limitations: Finetuning was unstable for some configurations, with some runs landing near chance accuracy especially for BERT. | Examples were truncated at 150 tokens, affecting roughly 1% of the data. | Some "mistakes" in development errors were actually correct but required a web search to verify. | Validation removed correct examples needing expert domain knowledge, narrowing the scope of "commonsense" the dataset captures.

Author: Nagel
Title: Up or Down? Adaptive Rounding for Post-Training Quantization
Contribution: AdaRound is a post-training weight-rounding method that adapts to data and task loss using a per-layer QUBO formulation solved via continuous relaxation, quantizing ResNet-18/50 weights to 4 bits within 1% accuracy drop.
Dataset: ImageNet (ILSVRC); Pascal VOC; MS COCO (used as alt calibration data)
Data Size: 1024 unlabeled ImageNet training images for ResNet18 ablations (2048 for the main literature comparison, 20k iterations); 512 images for DeepLabV3+ on Pascal VOC
Models Used: ResNet-18; ResNet-50; InceptionV3; MobileNetV2; DeepLabV3+ (MobileNetV2 backbone)
Evaluation Metrics: Top-1 Accuracy=69.68 (ResNet-18 32-bit ImageNet); Top-1 Accuracy=68.71 (ResNet-18 4-bit ImageNet); Top-1 Accuracy=75.23 (ResNet-50 4-bit ImageNet); Top-1 Accuracy=68.6 (ResNet-18 4-bit ImageNet) | other metrics: ImageNet top-1 validation accuracy (%); Mean Intersection over Union (mIOU) for semantic segmentation
Key Results: ResNet-18 at 4-bit weights (W4/A32) reaches 68.71% top-1 vs FP32 69.68% (drop ~0.97 pp) | ResNet-50 at 4-bit weights reaches 75.23% top-1 vs FP32 76.07% (drop ~0.84 pp) | MobileNetV2 at W4/A32 reaches 69.78% vs FP32 71.72%; nearest rounding collapses to 8.09% | DeepLabV3+ on Pascal VOC at W4/A8 reaches 70.86 mIOU vs FP32 72.94 (~2 pp drop) while nearest collapses to 6.09
Strengths: Recovers ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 4-bit weight accuracy to within 1% of FP32, a clear new state-of-the-art for PTQ. | Computationally fast: AdaRound on ResNet-18 finishes in 10 minutes on one GTX 1080 Ti. | Robust to calibration data: as few as 256 unlabeled images, even from out-of-distribution sets, recover within ~2% of FP32. | Theoretically grounded: derives the rounding objective from a Taylor expansion of the task loss into a per-layer QUBO.
Limitations: Step size and rounding are not jointly optimised; any change to step size produces a different QUBO problem. | The diagonal preactivation Hessian is an approximation; ignoring cross-layer interactions and treating diag entries as constant is a simplification. | Activation quantization uses only simple min-max scaling, which limits aggressiveness on activations.

Author: Aminabadi
Title: DeepSpeed Inference: Enabling Efficient Inference of Transformer Models at Unprecedented Scale
Venue: SC22: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis (arXiv preprint arXiv:2207.00032)
Contribution: DeepSpeed Inference is a comprehensive transformer inference system combining inference-optimized GPU kernels (with FP16 and INT8 GeMM), tensor and pipeline parallelism, MoE-specific optimizations, and ZeRO-Inference heterogeneous offloading to deliver up to 7.3x latency reduction and 25x larger servable model size.
Dataset: Synthetic GPT-style prompts (128-token input, 8 generated tokens for dense latency); Synthetic MoE prompts (128-token input, 100 generated tokens, batch size 8); Synthetic throughput workload (512-token input, 50 generated tokens)
Data Size: Synthetic prompts: 128 input tokens for latency benchmarks (8 or 100 generated tokens) and 512 input tokens for throughput (50 generated tokens); no calibration set used
Models Used: GPT-2 1.5B; GPT-Neo 2.7B; GPT-J 6B; GPT-13B; GPT-NeoX-20B; GPT-50B; GPT-87B; LM-175B (GPT-3 scale); LM-530B (MT-NLG scale); 1.3B+MoE-128 (52B total); 2.4B+MoE-128 (107.7B total); 8B+MoE-128 (349B total); 24B+MoE-128 (1064.9B total); 47B+MoE-128 (2024B total = 2T); DistilBERT (E.T. comparison); BERT (E.T. comparison)
Evaluation Metrics: Latency reduction (x_factor)=7.3 (MoE-1T 16-bit A100 40GB); Throughput improvement (x_factor)=1.5 (GPT-3 175B 16-bit A100 40GB); Model scale vs GPU-only (x_factor)=25.0 (MT-NLG 530B 16-bit A6000 48GB); Compute throughput (TFLOPS)=84.0 (MT-NLG 530B 16-bit A6000 48GB) | other metrics: End-to-end latency (ms); Token throughput (tokens/sec); Compute throughput (TFLOPS per GPU); Aggregate memory bandwidth (TB/sec); Speedup factor over FasterTransformer baseline
Key Results: DeepSpeed-INT8 reaches up to 1.95x latency speedup over FasterTransformer FP16 baseline at small batch sizes for dense GPT models | DeepSpeed-MoE delivers up to 7.3x lower per-token latency vs PyTorch baseline and serves a 1T-parameter MoE model under 25 ms on 256 GPUs | 1.51x throughput improvement over FasterTransformer for GPT-3 175B on 2x8 A100 nodes | ZeRO-Inference runs a 530B model on a single A6000 GPU at 84 TFLOPS (54% of 158.4 TFLOPS theoretical peak), 25x larger than GPU-only solutions | DeepSpeed-FP16 reduces dense-model latency by up to 1.55x at small batch sizes and 1.57x at larger batches over FasterTransformer FP16
Strengths: Comprehensive system covering kernel fusion, tensor and pipeline parallelism, MoE optimizations, and heterogeneous offloading in one stack. | Scales to 256 GPUs and serves a 1T-parameter MoE model under 25 ms, an unprecedented scale for inference. | ZeRO-Inference democratises massive-model inference on a single A6000 by streaming weights from DRAM and NVMe at 54 percent of peak. | Open-source release as part of Microsoft DeepSpeed library, allowing replication and integration by the community.
Limitations: INT8 path is not characterised for accuracy; the paper reports only latency and throughput, not perplexity or downstream metrics. | Hybrid scheduling is limited to batch size 24 due to a PyTorch AllReduce kernel issue that the authors leave to future work. | FasterTransformer baseline cannot be run with combined TP+PP for 530B, so comparison uses a TP-only baseline only. | Only 33 percent of peak memory bandwidth is reached on 256 GPUs, leaving substantial headroom that the authors acknowledge.

Author: Frantar
Title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
Contribution: GPTQ is a one-shot weight-only post-training quantization method using approximate second-order information that compresses 175B-parameter GPT models to 3-4 bits in about four GPU hours with negligible accuracy loss.
Dataset: C4; WikiText2; Penn Treebank (PTB); LAMBADA; ARC (Easy and Challenge); PIQA; SQuAD (BERT-base appendix); ImageNet (ResNet-18/50 ablation)
Data Size: 128 random 2048-token segments sampled from C4 for calibration
Models Used: OPT-125M; OPT-350M; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; OPT-175B; BLOOM-560M; BLOOM-1.1B; BLOOM-1.7B; BLOOM-3B; BLOOM-7.1B; BLOOM-176B; BERT-base; ResNet-18; ResNet-50
Evaluation Metrics: Quantization runtime (hours)=4.2 (OPT-175B C4); Perplexity=8.34 (OPT-175B 16-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=10.54 (OPT-175B 4-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=8.37 (OPT-175B 4-bit WikiText-2) | other metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy; Per-token latency (ms); Speedup factor over FP16; GPU memory / GPU count for inference
Key Results: OPT-175B at 4-bit GPTQ reaches WikiText2 PPL 8.37 vs FP16 8.34 (delta 0.03), while RTN drops to 10.54 | OPT-175B at 3-bit GPTQ reaches WikiText2 PPL 8.68 (vs 8.34 FP16); RTN collapses to 7.3e3 | End-to-end 3.24x decoding speedup on A100 80GB (230 ms FP16 to 71 ms 3-bit) for OPT-175B | End-to-end 4.53x speedup on A6000 48GB (589 ms FP16 to 130 ms 3-bit), reducing GPU count from 8 to 2 | GPTQ quantizes OPT-175B in 4.2h and BLOOM-176B in 3.8h on a single A100
Strengths: First method to quantize 100B+ parameter LLMs (OPT-175B, BLOOM-176B) to 3-4 bits in roughly four GPU hours with negligible perplexity loss. | Real end-to-end decoding speedups: 3.25x on A100 and 4.5x on A6000 over FP16 via custom mixed-precision GPU kernels. | Pushes one-shot extreme quantization to 2-bit and ternary regimes, with under 1.5 PPL drop on OPT-175B at 2.2-bit grouping. | Open-source code released, with reproducibility statement listing CUDA kernels and full evaluation pipeline.
Limitations: No speedup on the actual matrix multiplications because mainstream hardware lacks mixed FP16xINT4 multiply support. | Activations are not quantized, so memory and compute savings are limited to the weight stream. | Speedups come only from reduced memory movement, not from any reduction in arithmetic operations. | Quality is judged by perplexity only; bias and other secondary effects of compression are not studied.

Author: Xiao
Title: SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models
Venue: ICML 2023 (Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 202)
Contribution: SmoothQuant is a training-free W8A8 PTQ method that uses an offline mathematically equivalent per-channel scaling to migrate quantization difficulty from activations to weights for LLMs.
Dataset: LAMBADA; HellaSwag; PIQA; WinoGrande; OpenBookQA; RTE; COPA; WikiText; MMLU; MNLI; QNLI; The Pile (calibration)
Data Size: 512 random calibration sentences from the Pile pre-training dataset
Models Used: OPT-175B; OPT-6.7B / 13B / 30B / 66B (scaling study); BLOOM-176B; GLM-130B; MT-NLG 530B; OPT-IML-30B (instruction-tuned); LLaMA-7B/13B/30B/65B; Llama-2-7B/13B/70B; Falcon-7B/40B; Mistral-7B; Mixtral-8x7B
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy=74.7 (OPT-175B 8-bit LAMBADA); Average Accuracy=66.5 (OPT-175B 8-bit 7-task average); Average Accuracy=66.8 (OPT-175B 8-bit 7-task average); Speedup over FP16=1.42 (OPT-30B (1 GPU, BS=16, SeqLen=512) 8-bit A100 80GB) | other metrics: zero-shot accuracy; perplexity (WikiText); inference latency (ms); peak GPU memory (GB); speedup factor (vs FP16)
Key Results: OPT-175B average accuracy across 7 zero-shot tasks: FP16 66.9% vs SmoothQuant-O3 66.8% (−0.1pp); WikiText PPL 10.99 → 11.17 | BLOOM-176B average accuracy: FP16 68.2% vs SmoothQuant-O2 68.4%; GLM-130B FP16 73.8% vs SmoothQuant-O1 73.7% | Up to 1.56× inference speedup and ~2× memory saving over FP16 in FasterTransformer; 1.51× speedup and 1.96× memory in PyTorch on A100 | MT-NLG 530B served on 8 GPUs (vs 16 for FP16) at similar latency; e.g. SeqLen 1024: FP16 16-GPU 1707ms/1095GB vs INT8 8-GPU 1689ms/570GB
Strengths: Maintains FP16 accuracy on OPT-175B, BLOOM-176B and GLM-130B with INT8 W8A8, while baselines like W8A8 naive and ZeroQuant collapse. | Hardware-friendly: uses standard INT8 GEMM kernels via per-tensor static activation quantization, avoiding LLM.int8() mixed-precision overhead. | Delivers up to 1.56× speedup and ~2× memory saving and serves MT-NLG 530B on a single 8×A100 node. | Training-free with only 512 calibration sentences; one calibration generalises to all downstream zero-shot tasks.
Limitations: Migration strength α must be hand-tuned per model family (0.5 for OPT/BLOOM, 0.75 for GLM-130B, 0.6–0.9 for Llama/Falcon/Mistral). | GLM-130B needs additional 2% top-token clipping during static calibration to recover accuracy. | Per-tensor static O3 setting still loses ~0.8–1% accuracy on BLOOM-176B and GLM-130B versus FP16. | Direct comparison with weight-only methods like GPTQ is avoided due to incompatible kernels and serving frameworks.

Author: Dettmers
Title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
Contribution: LLM.int8() is a two-part Int8 inference procedure (vector-wise quantization plus mixed-precision decomposition that isolates emergent outlier features in 16-bit) that quantizes transformers up to 175B parameters with no performance loss and halves inference memory.
Dataset: C4 (validation); WinoGrande; HellaSwag; PIQA; LAMBADA; EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness; Books / English Wikipedia / CC-News / OpenWebText / CC-Stories / English CC100 (pretraining corpus); WMT14+WMT16 (NMT training appendix); GLUE (RoBERTa-large finetuning appendix)
Data Size: C4 validation perplexity for models 125M-13B; zeroshot evaluation on OPT models 125M-175B; 2048-token sequences for outlier analysis (about 150,000 outliers per sequence at 6.7B)
Models Used: Fairseq dense LM 125M; Fairseq dense LM 1.3B; Fairseq dense LM 2.7B; Fairseq dense LM 6.7B; Fairseq dense LM 13B; OPT-125M / 1.3B / 2.7B / 6.7B / 13B / 30B / 66B / 175B; BLOOM-176B; GPT-2 (117M / 345M / 762M / 1.5B); GPT-J 6B; RoBERTa-large (finetuning appendix)
Evaluation Metrics: Performance retention vs FP16=no degradation (OPT-175B 8-bit C4); Memory reduction factor=1.96 (BLOOM-176B 8-bit N/A); Perplexity degradation (%)=600-1000% (Transformer-LM 16-bit C4); Perplexity=12.45 (Transformer-13B 8-bit C4) | other metrics: C4 validation perplexity (PPL); Mean zeroshot accuracy (WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, LAMBADA); Top-1 attention softmax probability; Memory footprint reduction factor; Per-token end-to-end inference latency (ms)
Key Results: OPT-13B C4 PPL: FP32=12.45, Int8 absmax=19.08, Int8 vector-wise=16.48, LLM.int8()=12.45 (no degradation) | LLM.int8() preserves zeroshot accuracy from 125M up to 175B OPT, while 8-bit absmax vector-wise degenerates to random performance after 6.7B parameters | Removing the about 7 outlier feature dimensions (~0.1% of features) drops top-1 softmax probability from ~40% to ~20% and increases perplexity by 600-1000% | Phase shift at 6.7B parameters: outliers go from 65% to 100% of layers and 35% to 75% of sequence dimensions, co-occurring with quantization failure | BLOOM-176B end-to-end per-token latency: bf16 baseline 239 ms (8xA100) vs LLM.int8() 247 ms on only 3xA100 (similar speed, fewer GPUs)
Strengths: First Int8 method to preserve full predictive performance for 175B-parameter transformers, including OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B. | Halves inference memory and lets BLOOM-176B run on a single consumer GPU server, broadening access for low-resource researchers. | Provides the first descriptive analysis of emergent outlier features that explains why prior 8-bit methods fail at the 6.7B scale. | Open-source bitsandbytes library and Hugging Face integration, making the method easy to reproduce and apply to existing models.
Limitations: Studied only Int8; the FP8 data type and its potential accuracy or speed gains are left to future work. | Method is only validated up to 175B parameters; emergent properties at larger scales could break the procedure. | Attention function itself is not quantized, limiting compute savings beyond memory bandwidth reduction. | Quantization overhead actually slows inference for models smaller than 6.7B parameters compared to FP16.

Author: Touvron
Title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
Contribution: Llama 2 is an open-release family of pretrained and fine-tuned LLMs (7B, 13B, 70B) optimized via SFT and RLHF for dialogue, with safety tuning and Ghost Attention.
Dataset: HumanEval; MBPP; PIQA; SIQA; HellaSwag; WinoGrande; ARC (easy and challenge); OpenBookQA; CommonsenseQA; NaturalQuestions; TriviaQA; SQuAD; QuAC; BoolQ; GSM8K; MATH; MMLU; BIG-Bench Hard (BBH); AGI Eval; TruthfulQA; ToxiGen
Data Size: 2 trillion pretraining tokens; 27,540 SFT annotations; ~1.4M binary human preference comparisons for RLHF reward modeling
Models Used: Llama 2 7B; Llama 2 13B; Llama 2 34B; Llama 2 70B; Llama 2-Chat 7B; Llama 2-Chat 13B; Llama 2-Chat 70B; Llama 1 (7B/13B/33B/65B, baselines); MPT (7B/30B, baseline); Falcon (7B/40B, baseline); GPT-3.5 (closed baseline); GPT-4 (closed baseline); PaLM 540B (closed baseline); PaLM-2-L (closed baseline)
Evaluation Metrics: Pretraining tokens=2T (Llama-2 Pretraining corpus); Win rate vs ChatGPT (%)=36.0 (Llama-2-Chat-70B Human Eval (helpfulness ~4000 prompts)); Tie rate vs ChatGPT (%)=31.5 (Llama-2-Chat-70B Human Eval (helpfulness ~4000 prompts)); Win rate vs MPT-7B-chat (%)=60.0 (Llama-2-Chat-7B Human Eval (helpfulness)) | other metrics: Accuracy (multiple-choice / classification benchmarks); pass@1 (HumanEval / MBPP code); Helpfulness win-rate (human + GPT-4); Safety violation percentage (human eval, ~2,000 adversarial prompts); TruthfulQA truthful-and-informative %
Key Results: Llama 2 70B reaches MMLU 68.9, BBH 51.2, AGI Eval 54.2, beating all open-source baselines (MPT-30B, Falcon-40B, Llama 1 65B) | Llama 2 70B improves over Llama 1 65B by ~5 points on MMLU and ~8 points on BBH | Llama 2 70B closes ground on GPT-3.5: MMLU 68.9 vs 70.0 and GSM8K 56.8 vs 57.1 (still a gap on coding) | Pretraining cost: 3.3M GPU-hours on A100-80GB and 539 tCO2eq emitted (100% offset by Meta)
Strengths: Open release of competitive 7B/13B/70B base + chat models with permissive license enables reproducible research and commercial use. | Architectural upgrades over Llama 1: 4k context, 40% more pretraining tokens, and grouped-query attention for inference scaling. | Detailed safety methodology: red-teaming, safety-tuning, iterative RLHF, and Ghost Attention for multi-turn dialogue control. | Closes much of the gap to GPT-3.5 on MMLU and GSM8K and is on par with PaLM-540B on most benchmarks.
Limitations: Knowledge frozen post-pretraining; the model can produce non-factual content and hallucinations. | Predominantly English; performance in other languages is fragile and should be used with caution. | Safety tuning sometimes overshoots, causing the model to refuse benign requests or add excessive safety caveats. | Can still emit harmful, offensive, or biased content because pretraining data is drawn from public web sources.

Author: Chee
Title: QuIP: 2-Bit Quantization of Large Language Models With Guarantees
Contribution: QuIP is a post-training weight-only quantization method that uses incoherence processing via random orthogonal matrices to enable the first viable 2-bit LLM quantization, paired with adaptive rounding (LDLQ) and theoretical guarantees.
Dataset: C4; WikiText2; Penn Treebank (PTB); LAMBADA; ARC Easy; PiQA; StoryCloze
Data Size: 128 random 2048-token segments from C4 (calibration set)
Models Used: OPT-125m; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; Llama 2 70B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity=123.908 (LLaMA-2-70B 2-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=6.326 (LLaMA-2-70B 2-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=8.937 (LLaMA-2-70B 2-bit C4); Perplexity=71.7 (OPT-30B 2-bit WikiText-2) | other metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy; Per-token throughput (ms)
Key Results: Llama 2 70B at 2-bit with QuIP reaches WikiText PPL 6.326 vs 16-bit 3.319, while OPTQ collapses to 123.908 at 2-bit | OPT-30B at 2-bit with QuIP reaches WikiText PPL 11.48 vs 16-bit 9.56, while OPTQ degrades to 71.70 | QuIP is about 1.5x slower than OPTQ at inference: 81 ms/token vs 53 ms/token on OPT-66B (A6000) | Random permutation in fast orthogonal multiplication reduces 2-bit perplexity by 74.2 points on OPT-125m (averaged over WikiText2/PTB/C4)
Strengths: First PTQ method to make 2-bit weight quantization viable across LLM sizes (including OPT-66B and Llama 2 70B). | Provides the first theoretical analysis for an LLM-scale quantization algorithm and shows the analysis also covers OPTQ. | Incoherence processing improves every rounding method tested, including plain nearest rounding, at 2 bits. | Code is open-sourced on GitHub for full reproducibility.
Limitations: QuIP inference is about 1.5x slower than OPTQ because incoherence processing is implemented in PyTorch. | Adaptive rounding proxy treats each layer in isolation; cross-layer interactions are not modelled. | QuIP-RG variant sometimes beats QuIP but the authors note further study is required to evaluate it.

Author: Yao
Title: ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers
Contribution: ZeroQuant is an end-to-end post-training quantization and inference pipeline that pairs group-wise weight and token-wise activation quantization with a layer-by-layer knowledge distillation method and optimized INT8 GPU kernels for BERT and GPT-3-style models up to 20B parameters.
Dataset: GLUE (CoLA, MNLI, MRPC, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, STS-B); Lambada; PIQA; OpenBookQA; ReCoRD; HellaSwag; TriviaQA; WebQS; Winogrande; ARC (Easy and Challenge); ANLI (R1/R2/R3); RACE-h; BoolQ; COPA; WSC; MultiRC; WikiText-2; WikiText-103; Penn Treebank (PTB); PILE (LKD calibration / GPT-3 pretraining); Wikipedia (HuggingFace, LKD without original data)
Data Size: BERT calibration: batch size 32, sequence length 128, momentum 0.95 over 100 iterations; GPT-3 calibration: batch size 8, sequence length 2048; LKD: 100-1600 iterations depending on model.
Models Used: BERT-base; BERT-large; GPT-3-style 350M; GPT-3-style 1.3B; GPT-J 6B; GPT-NeoX 20B
Evaluation Metrics: Average Accuracy=82.35 (BERT-base 4-bit GLUE); Speedup over FP16=5.19 (BERT-base 8-bit A100 (BS128, SeqLen128)); Speedup over FP16=4.16 (GPT-3-350M 8-bit A100 (50-token gen)); Speedup over FP16=3.67 (GPT-J-6B 8-bit A100 (50-token gen)) | other metrics: GLUE accuracy (Matthews / accuracy / F1 / Pearson-Spearman); Zero-shot accuracy (19 tasks average); Perplexity (Wikitext-2 / Wikitext-103 / PTB); End-to-end latency (ms); Speedup factor over FP16
Key Results: BERT-base W8A8 ZeroQuant reaches 83.75 GLUE average vs 83.95 FP16 baseline (delta 0.20) at 0 s calibration cost, while standard PTQ falls to 77.41 | BERT-base W4/8A16 ZeroQuant-LKD reaches 82.35 GLUE average (vs PTQ 33.11) in 31 s per task, ~93.5x cheaper than INT8 QAT (2900 s) | GPT-3 350M W8A8 ZeroQuant reaches Wikitext-2 PPL 21.7 vs 21.5 FP16 (delta 0.2), while W8A8 PTQ degrades to 26.2 | Up to 5.19x INT8 speedup on BERT-base and 4.16x on GPT-3 350M end-to-end on a single 40G A100 vs FP16 | GPT-NeoX 20B W8A8/16 cuts latency from 2x65ms to 1x25ms and halves GPU count, giving 5.2x better efficiency at matched accuracy (Ave. 50.4 vs 50.5) | GPT-J 6B W8A8 reaches 10.51 PPL on WikiText-2 vs 10.35 FP16 with 3.67x latency speedup (29.13 ms to 7.94 ms)
Strengths: Group-wise weight and token-wise activation quantization recover near-FP16 accuracy on BERT and GPT-3-style models with zero calibration cost. | Layer-by-layer knowledge distillation enables INT4/INT8 mixed-precision compression even without access to the original training data. | Custom CUTLASS INT8 kernels and operator fusion give real end-to-end speedups up to 5.19x on BERT and 5.2x on GPT-NeoX 20B. | Scales to 20B-parameter open-source models, halving the GPU count required for GPT-NeoX 20B inference from 2 A100 to 1 A100.
Limitations: Self-attention input activations of GPT-NeoX 20B must stay in FP16 because INT8 there causes large accuracy loss; root cause is conjectured but not verified. | INT4/INT8 mixed precision still loses accuracy on small or generation-heavy tasks such as RTE and Wikitext-2 even with LKD. | Hyper-parameters for LKD are kept fixed across all tasks; the authors note tuning could change results. | INT4 weights are only applied to FFC; MHSA weights stay at INT8, so the average bitwidth is higher than pure INT4.

Author: Lin
Title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for On-Device LLM Compression and Acceleration
Contribution: AWQ is a hardware-friendly low-bit weight-only PTQ method that protects the top 1% salient channels using activation-aware per-channel scaling, with no backpropagation, and is paired with TinyChat to deliver 3-4x edge speedup over FP16.
Dataset: WikiText-2; The Pile; PubMed Abstracts (Pile subset); Enron Emails; COCO Captions; MBPP; GSM8K; Vicuna-Bench (80 GPT-4 questions); VQAv2 / GQA / VizWiz / SQA-I / VQA-T / POPE / MME / MMB / SEED / LLaVA-Bench / MM-Vet (VILA suite)
Data Size: 16 sequences for AWQ calibration vs 192 for GPTQ on OPT-6.7B (10x smaller); 5k samples for COCO captioning eval; 1k samples for PubMed/Enron eval
Models Used: OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; Llama-2-7B; Llama-2-13B; Llama-2-70B; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2; Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1; Vicuna-7B / 13B; OpenFlamingo-9B; LLaVA-13B; VILA-7B / VILA-13B; CodeLlama-7B-Instruct-hf; Falcon-7B / Falcon-180B; MPT; StarCoder
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity=6.24 (Llama-2-7B 3-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=3.74 (Llama-2-70B 3-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=5.6 (Llama-2-7B 4-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=3.41 (Llama-2-70B 4-bit WikiText-2) | other metrics: Perplexity (WikiText-2); CIDEr (COCO Captioning); GPT-4 evaluation score (Vicuna); pass@1 / pass@10 (MBPP); Accuracy (GSM8K, VQAv2, GQA, VizWiz, SQA-I, VQA-T, POPE, MME, MMB, SEED, LLaVA-Bench, MM-Vet)
Key Results: Llama-2-7B at INT3-g128: AWQ PPL 6.24 vs FP16 5.47 (GPTQ 6.43, GPTQ-R 6.42, RTN 6.66) on WikiText-2 | Llama-2-70B at INT4-g128: AWQ PPL 3.41 vs FP16 3.32 (Delta 0.09) | OpenFlamingo-9B at INT4-g128 32-shot: AWQ CIDEr 80.53 vs FP16 81.70 (degradation reduced from 4.57 to 1.17) | TinyChat with 4-bit AWQ delivers 3.2-3.3x average speedup over Huggingface FP16 across desktop, laptop and mobile GPUs | TinyChat reaches 3.9x speedup on RTX 4090 desktop and 3.5x on Jetson Orin mobile GPU vs FP16 Huggingface
Strengths: Hardware-friendly: avoids mixed-precision by using per-channel scaling, so 4-bit weights stay in a uniform integer format. | Generalist: no backpropagation or reconstruction, so it does not overfit calibration data and works for instruction-tuned and multi-modal LLMs. | Data-efficient: needs roughly 10x less calibration data than GPTQ (16 vs 192 sequences) for OPT-6.7B INT3. | Practical edge speedup: TinyChat delivers 3-4x measured speedup on desktop, laptop, and mobile GPUs, including Llama-2-70B on a single Jetson Orin.
Limitations: Does not quantize activations - W4A16 keeps activations in FP16 and only reduces weight memory. | Selecting the optimal scale needs a small grid search (size 20) over alpha, adding tuning cost per layer. | INT2 quantization on its own is not enough; AWQ has to be combined with GPTQ to recover usable PPL on OPT. | On-the-fly dequantization is still costly on SIMD CPUs and needs platform-specific weight packing.

Author: Kim
Title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization
Contribution: SqueezeLLM is a post-training weight-only PTQ framework that uses sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization plus Dense-and-Sparse decomposition to achieve near-lossless 3-bit LLM compression and up to 2.3x speedup on A6000.
Dataset: C4; WikiText2; MMLU; Vicuna instruction-following benchmark
Data Size: 100 random calibration samples (from Vicuna training set for Vicuna models, C4 training set otherwise); chunk size 2048; data efficiency study shows 10 samples are enough.
Models Used: LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; LLaMA2-7B; LLaMA2-13B; LLaMA2-70B; OPT; Vicuna-7B (v1.1, v1.3); Vicuna-13B (v1.1, v1.3); Vicuna-33B (v1.3)
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity=7.75 (LLaMA-7B 3-bit C4); Speedup over FP16=2.3 (LLaMA-7B 3-bit C4); Perplexity=28.26 (LLaMA-7B 3-bit C4); Perplexity=7.56 (LLaMA-7B 3-bit C4) | other metrics: Perplexity (PPL); MMLU zero-shot accuracy; GPT-4 ranked instruction-following win/tie/loss; Latency (seconds for 128/1024 tokens); Peak GPU memory (GB)
Key Results: 3-bit LLaMA-7B (dense-only) PPL on C4 = 7.75 vs FP16 7.08; 0.45% sparsity drops it to 7.56 (gap 0.48); RTN baseline is 28.26. | 3-bit LLaMA-7B reduces perplexity gap from FP16 by up to 2.1x compared to GPTQ/AWQ at the same memory budget. | Up to 2.3x decoding speedup over FP16 on A6000 (3-bit dense-only LLaMA-7B latency 1.5s vs 3.2s baseline for 128 tokens). | 4-bit LLaMA-7B (0.45% sparse) PPL = 7.18 on C4 / 5.77 on WikiText-2 vs FP16 7.08/5.68 (~0.1 PPL gap) at 3.95x compression.
Strengths: Sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization cuts 3-bit LLaMA-7B C4 PPL from 28.26 (RTN) to 7.75, with no retraining. | Dense-and-Sparse decomposition isolates 0.45% outlier and sensitive weights to enable near-lossless 3-bit compression. | Custom LUT-based CUDA kernels deliver up to 2.3x A6000 speedup and 1.5-2.5x A100 speedup over FP16. | Data-efficient calibration: only 10 samples needed to compute Fisher information, vs 100-200 for GPTQ/AWQ.
Limitations: Empirical results focus on generation tasks; framework not yet assessed on non-decoder architectures. | Higher quantization-time memory than GPTQ because Fisher information matrix needs gradient back-propagation. | Dense-only 2-bit SqueezeLLM lags behind OmniQuant on 13B/70B; sparsity overhead is needed to recover accuracy. | Sparse component needs a custom balanced kernel; standard CSR adds over 100% latency overhead.

Author: Dettmers
Title: SpQR: A Sparse-Quantized Representation for Near-Lossless LLM Weight Compression
Contribution: SpQR is a hybrid sparse-quantized PTQ format that isolates outlier weights at 16-bit and quantizes the rest to 3-4 bits, reaching near-lossless (<1% perplexity loss) compression of LLaMA and Falcon LLMs.
Dataset: WikiText-2; Penn Treebank; C4; WinoGrande; PiQA; HellaSwag; ARC-easy; ARC-challenge; RedPajama (calibration for LLaMA); RefinedWeb (calibration for Falcon)
Data Size: 128 calibration sequences of 2048 tokens each (sensitivity analysis on LLaMA-65B with C4)
Models Used: LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; Falcon-7B; Falcon-40B; OPT-6.7B / 13B / 30B / 66B (appendix F)
Evaluation Metrics: Speedup over FP16=1.15 (LLaMA-33B 4-bit Consumer GPU 24GB); Memory compression factor=4.0 (LLaMA family 4-bit WikiText2); Relative perplexity error vs FP16=1.0 (LLaMA family 4-bit WikiText2); Speedup over FP16=1.25 (LLaMA family 4-bit A100) | other metrics: Perplexity (WikiText2, C4, PTB); Zero-shot accuracy (WinoGrande, PiQA, HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c); Average bits per parameter; Inference tokens/second (latency proxy)
Key Results: LLaMA-65B at SpQR 4.71 avg bits: WikiText2 PPL 3.57 vs FP16 3.53 (Δ 0.04, near-lossless) | LLaMA-7B at SpQR ~3.94 bits: WikiText2 PPL 5.87 vs GPTQ-4bit 6.13 and RTN-4bit 6.43 | Falcon-40B at SpQR 4.46 avg bits: WikiText2 PPL 5.26 vs FP16 5.23 (within 1%) | Optimized SpQR inference: 20-30% faster than FP16 baseline on A100 (e.g. LLaMA-30B 22 vs 19 tok/s)
Strengths: First PTQ method to reach near-lossless 3-4 bit compression with under 1% perplexity loss across LLaMA and Falcon scales. | Custom GPU sparse-dense kernel makes 3-4 bit SpQR 20-30% faster than FP16 inference on A100. | Bilevel quantization of scales and zero-points enables very small group sizes (8-32) cheaply. | Provides hardware-targeted recipes mapping LLaMA size + bit-width to phones, laptops, RTX and server GPUs.
Limitations: Authors only measure perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, not actual generation quality. | Sparse and dense matmul are not fused, which leaves inference time on the table. | Outliers cost ~32 bits each (16-bit value + 16-bit column index), no compression of outlier indices.

Author: Shao
Title: OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated Quantization for Large Language Models
Contribution: OmniQuant is a differentiable PTQ method for LLMs that learns weight clipping (LWC) and equivalent transformation (LET) parameters via block-wise error minimization, working for both weight-only and weight-activation quantization.
Dataset: WikiText2; PTB; C4; PIQA; ARC; BoolQ; HellaSwag; Winogrande; Vicuna-Bench
Data Size: 128 randomly selected 2048-token segments from WikiText2
Models Used: OPT (125M-66B); LLaMA-1 (7B-65B); LLaMA-2 (7B-70B); Falcon-180B; LLaMA-2-chat
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity=13.21 (LLaMA-1-13B 2-bit WikiText2); Quantization time (hours)=1.6 (LLaMA-2-7B 4-bit A100-40G); Quantization time (hours)=14.4 (LLaMA-2-70B 4-bit A100-40G); Accuracy=52.65 (LLaMA-1-7B 4-bit Zero-shot Avg (6 tasks)) | other metrics: Perplexity (PPL) on WikiText2; Zero-shot accuracy; Win rate (GPT-4 evaluation, Vicuna); Inference speed (tokens/s) and memory (GB)
Key Results: LLaMA-13B at W2A16: OmniQuant PPL 13.21 vs GPTQ 5.5e3 (huge gap at 2-bit weight-only) | LLaMA-1-7B at W4A4: OmniQuant average zero-shot acc 52.65% vs SmoothQuant 38.41%, surpassing LLM-QAT (41.27%) by +6.22% | W4A4 average accuracy gain across LLaMA models: +4.99% to +11.80% over best prior PTQ baseline | LLaMA-7B W4A16g128 deployment via MLC-LLM: 134.2 tokens/s vs FP16 69.2 tokens/s (1.94x faster) and 3.8GB weight memory vs 12.6GB
Strengths: Achieves QAT-level accuracy with PTQ-level training cost: LLaMA-2-70B quantized in 16h on a single A100-40G with only 128 samples. | Versatile across configurations: handles W4A4, W6A6, W4A16, W3A16, W2A16 for both weight-only and weight-activation quantization. | Adds zero deployment overhead: learnable clipping and equivalent transform fuse into quantized weights, leaving inference graph unchanged. | Generalizes to instruction-tuned LLaMA-2-chat with strong win rate vs RTN and parity or better than AWQ at W3A16g128.
Limitations: Training time is roughly 5x slower than GPTQ, even though it stays much faster than QAT methods. | MLC-LLM kernel support for INT3/INT2 inference is suboptimal, limiting actual speedup of low-bit configs. | Real-device deployment is shown only for weight-only quantization, since W4A4 and W6A6 lack hardware support. | Learnable equivalent transformation gives only slight gain on LLaMA weight-only, indicating it is not always essential.

Author: Jaiswal
Title: Compressing LLMs: The Truth is Rarely Pure and Never Simple
Contribution: Introduces LLM-KICK, a knowledge-intensive benchmark that re-evaluates SoTA pruning and quantization methods beyond perplexity, showing pruning fails at modest sparsity while quantization is more successful but still drops on knowledge tasks.
Dataset: FreebaseQA; MMLU; TriviaQA; CNN/DailyMail; MT-Bench; WikiText
Data Size: FreebaseQA, MMLU, TriviaQA, MT-Bench (80 prompts across categories), CNN/DailyMail (3 subsets of 100 articles each: small <=470 words, medium 470-790, large >=790)
Models Used: Vicuna-7B; Vicuna-13B; Vicuna-33B; LLaMA-1 7B; LLaMA-2 7B
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy=61.02 (Vicuna-7B 8-bit FreebaseQA); Accuracy=13.99 (Vicuna-7B FreebaseQA); Accuracy=46.7 (Vicuna-7B 16-bit MMLU); Accuracy=31.7 (Vicuna-13B MMLU) | other metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Factoid-QA accuracy (FreebaseQA); MCR-QA accuracy (MMLU); ICRA-QA accuracy (TriviaQA open/closed-book); Summarization quality (GPT-4 Judge: coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance)
Key Results: GPTQ 8-bit on Vicuna-7B Factoid-QA reaches 60.14% vs LLM-int8 61.02% and AWQ 60.31% (dense baseline ~65.4%) | GPTQ 8-bit on Vicuna-7B MMLU reaches 47.10%, AWQ 47.18%, LLM-int8 47.82% (vs dense 47.1%) | All SoTA pruning methods catastrophically fail on FreebaseQA at 50% sparsity (Magnitude 13.99%, SparseGPT 42.86%, Wanda 44.66%) vs dense 65.44% | Vicuna-13B with 46% sparsity (Magnitude/Wanda/SparseGPT, ~7B params) hits MMLU 31.7% / 45.3% / 46.3% vs dense Vicuna-7B 46.7% — large-sparse not better than small-dense | Even 8-bit GPTQ shows ~8-10% drop on Factoid-QA, indicating non-aggressive quantization remains unsolved
Strengths: First holistic benchmark (LLM-KICK) that exposes how perplexity hides large knowledge losses in compressed LLMs across factoid QA, reasoning, retrieval, summarization, and instruction following. | Compares four leading methods (Magnitude, SparseGPT, Wanda, GPTQ) plus AWQ and LLM.int8 across three model scales (7B, 13B, 33B) and two model families (Vicuna, LLaMA-2). | Shows quantization preserves knowledge much better than pruning, while pruning still works for in-context retrieval and summarization at high sparsity. | Reproducible: averages 3 independent runs per cell and releases code at github.com/VITA-Group/llm-kick.
Limitations: Evaluation restricted to Vicuna decoder-only models due to license; limits generality across architectures. | Does not test parameter-efficient recovery; future work to use LoRA/QLoRA is acknowledged but not done. | GPT-4 is the judge for summarization and instruction following, which adds dependence on a closed proprietary scorer.

Author: Dubey
Title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
Contribution: Llama 3 is a herd of dense Transformer foundation models (8B, 70B, 405B parameters) with up to 128K context, pre-trained on 15.6T tokens, openly released and competitive with GPT-4.
Dataset: MMLU; MMLU-Pro; HumanEval; MBPP; GSM8K; MATH; ARC Challenge; DROP; SQuAD V2; QuAC; RACE; CommonSenseQA; PiQA; SiQA; OpenBookQA; WinoGrande; AGIEval; BIG-Bench Hard; QuALITY; IFEval; GPQA; BFCL; Nexus; InfiniteBench; NIH/Multi-needle; MGSM
Data Size: Pre-training corpus of about 15T multilingual tokens; flagship model trained on 15.6T text tokens.
Models Used: Llama 3 8B; Llama 3 8B Instruct; Llama 3 70B; Llama 3 70B Instruct; Llama 3.1 8B; Llama 3.1 8B Instruct; Llama 3.1 70B; Llama 3.1 70B Instruct; Llama 3.1 405B; Llama 3.1 405B Instruct; Llama Guard 3
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy=69.4 (Llama-3-8B MMLU (5-shot)); Accuracy=83.6 (Llama-3-70B MMLU (5-shot)); Accuracy=87.3 (Llama-3-405B MMLU (5-shot)); Pass@1=72.6 (Llama-3-8B HumanEval (0-shot)) | other metrics: 95% confidence interval; Pass@1 (HumanEval); Exact Match (DROP); Throughput (tokens/sec); Reward model score distribution
Key Results: Llama 3 405B Instruct reaches MMLU 87.3 (5-shot) and 88.6 (0-shot CoT), competitive with GPT-4 (85.1) and GPT-4o (89.1) | Llama 3 405B Instruct scores 89.0 on HumanEval (0-shot) and 96.8 on GSM8K (8-shot CoT) | FP8 quantization yields up to 50% throughput improvement during pre-fill on H100 vs BF16 for Llama 3 405B | int8 Llama Guard 3 keeps English F1 at 0.936 vs 0.939 non-quantized while shrinking size by more than 40%
Strengths: Open release of pre-trained and post-trained 8B, 70B, and 405B models with 128K context, enabling community research and reproducibility. | Flagship 405B model performs on par with leading models like GPT-4 across many tasks. | Reports 95% confidence intervals on benchmark scores, improving statistical rigor. | Open release of FP8 inference kernels and quantized Llama Guard 3 supports efficient deployment.
Limitations: Standard benchmarks do not adequately reflect FP8 quantization effects; the model can produce corrupted responses without scaling-factor upper bound. | FP8 quantization quality is sensitive; first and last Transformer layers and attention layers are kept in higher precision. | Llama 3 may still generate harmful content for non-English languages and under skilled adversarial prompting. | Adding system safeguards trades higher refusal rates of benign prompts for lower violation rates.

Author: Tseng
Title: QuIP#: Even Better LLM Quantization with Hadamard Incoherence and Lattice Codebooks
Contribution: QuIP# is a weight-only PTQ method that combines Randomized Hadamard Transform incoherence processing, an E_8 lattice (E8P) vector-quantization codebook with BlockLDLQ rounding, and inter-layer fine-tuning to reach state-of-the-art at 2-4 bits with fast GPU inference.
Dataset: WikiText-2; C4; RedPajama 1T (calibration / fine-tuning); ARC-Challenge (zeroshot); ARC-Easy (zeroshot); PIQA (zeroshot); WinoGrande (zeroshot); BoolQ (zeroshot, appendix)
Data Size: Hessians: 6144 calibration sequences from RedPajama 1T at native context length (2048 for Llama 1, 4096 for Llama 2). Fine-tuning: 256 train + 128 validation sequences from RedPajama 1T.
Models Used: Llama 1 7B; Llama 1 13B; Llama 1 30B; Llama 1 65B; Llama 2 7B; Llama 2 13B; Llama 2 70B; Mixtral 8x7B; Falcon 180B; Llama 2 70B Chat (qualitative example generations only)
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (ctx 4096)=3.91 (Llama-2-70B 2-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity (ctx 4096)=3.35 (Llama-2-70B 3-bit WikiText-2); % Peak Memory Bandwidth=56.84 (Llama-2-70B 2-bit Llama RTX 4090 (FlashAttention)); Throughput (tok/s)=106.3 (Llama-2-7B 2-bit Llama RTX 4090 (HuggingFace)) | other metrics: WikiText-2 perplexity; C4 perplexity; Zeroshot accuracy (LM Eval); Generation throughput (tokens/sec)
Key Results: Llama-2-70B at 2 bits with QuIP# reaches WikiText-2 PPL 4.16 vs FP16 3.32 (ctx 2048) | Llama-2-70B at 3 bits with QuIP# reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.35 vs FP16 3.12 (ctx 4096), beating AQLM 3.04-bit at 3.36 PPL | Llama-2-70B at 2 bits achieves 32.74 tok/s and 56.84% peak memory bandwidth on RTX 4090 (FlashAttention impl.) | QuIP# 2-bit Llama-2-7B reaches 106.3 tok/s vs FP16 33.1 tok/s (~3.2x speedup) on RTX 4090 via HuggingFace impl.
Strengths: First PTQ method where 3-bit models scale better than theoretical lossless 4-bit models on Llama 2. | Hardware-friendly E8P codebook fits in 1 KiB of GPU L1 cache, enabling >50% peak memory bandwidth at 2 bits. | RHT incoherence processing improves the theoretical bound on incoherence and runs in O(n log n) time. | Fine-tuning step can quantize Llama 2 70B in roughly 100 GPU-hours, far cheaper than QAT (LLM-QAT 960 GPU-hours).
Limitations: Method is restricted to weight-only quantization; activations stay in FP16. | RHT requires power-of-2 dimensions or special factorisations; non-supported sizes need an alternative RFFT. | Authors note QuIP# fast-inference design choices restrict quantization quality, so better quality is possible but slower. | RFFT incoherence variant performs slightly worse than RHT in practice (Table 1).

Author: Hooper
Title: KVQuant: Towards 10 Million Context Length LLM Inference with KV Cache Quantization
Contribution: KVQuant is a sub-4-bit KV cache PTQ method using per-channel pre-RoPE Key quantization, sensitivity-weighted non-uniform datatypes (nuqX), and per-vector dense-and-sparse outlier handling, enabling 10M context length LLaMA-7B inference on an 8-GPU system with under 0.1 perplexity loss.
Dataset: Wikitext-2; C4; LongBench; RULER; Passkey Retrieval
Data Size: 16 calibration samples of sequence length 2K from the Wikitext-2 training set
Models Used: LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; Llama-2-7B; Llama-2-13B; Llama-2-70B; Llama-3-8B; Llama-3-70B; Mistral-7B; LLaMA-2-7B-32K; Llama-2-70B-32K LongLoRA
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity=5.68 (LLaMA-7B 16-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=5.72 (LLaMA-7B 4-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=5.69 (LLaMA-7B 4-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=5.87 (LLaMA-7B 3-bit WikiText-2) | other metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Passkey retrieval success rate; LongBench task scores; RULER accuracy; Latency (microseconds)
Key Results: LLaMA-7B at 3-bit (KVQuant-3bit-1%): Wikitext-2 PPL 5.75 vs fp16 5.68 (Δ 0.07) | LLaMA-7B at 2-bit (KVQuant-2bit-1%): Wikitext-2 PPL 6.01 vs fp16 5.68 with 6.9× memory savings | Up to 1.7× speedup over fp16 matvec for Value at l=16K on A6000 (LLaMA-2-7B-32K, nuq4-1%) | Enables 1M context length LLaMA-7B on a single A100-80GB GPU and 10M context on 8-GPU system (nuq2)
Strengths: Sub-4-bit KV cache quantization with under 0.1 PPL degradation across LLaMA, Llama-2, Llama-3, Mistral models. | Enables 1M context on single A100 GPU and 10M context on an 8-GPU system for LLaMA-7B. | Custom CUDA kernels deliver up to 1.7× speedup vs fp16 matvec on A6000. | Code released at github.com/SqueezeAILab/KVQuant for reproducibility.
Limitations: Latency benchmarks focus on memory-bandwidth-bound generation, not prompt processing where many KV pairs compress at once. | Does not address training of long-context models (>100K), only inference. | Sparse matrix memory allocation is inefficient; appending new tokens requires copying prior data.

Author: Wang
Title: DecodingTrust: A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models
Venue: NeurIPS 2023 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track, Outstanding Paper)
Contribution: DecodingTrust is a comprehensive benchmark assessing GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and six open LLMs across eight trustworthiness dimensions: toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, OOD robustness, robustness to adversarial demonstrations, privacy, machine ethics, and fairness.
Dataset: REALTOXICITYPROMPTS; LLM-generated challenging toxic prompts (1.2K, GPT-3.5/GPT-4); DecodingTrust Stereotype dataset (1,152 prompts, 16 topics, 24 demographic groups); AdvGLUE; AdvGLUE++ (authors' new adversarial set); RealtimeQA (OOD knowledge, 2020 vs 2023 events); Enron Email Dataset; Constructed PII conversation dataset (18 PII types); ETHICS (commonsense morality, short and long); Jiminy Cricket; Adult (UCI tabular fairness dataset)
Data Size: Eight perspectives totaling >270K prompts, e.g. toxicity uses two 1.2K subsets of REALTOXICITYPROMPTS plus 1.2K LLM-generated, stereotype 1,152 prompts, AdvGLUE++ 11.5K examples, Enron ~3,300 (name,email) pairs, ETHICS 3,885 test, Adult 200 test samples per setting.
Models Used: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314); GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301); GPT-3 Ada / Curie / Davinci; Llama-v2-7B-Chat; Vicuna-7B; Alpaca-7B; MPT-7B; Falcon-7B; RedPajama-INCITE-7B-Instruct; Vicuna-13B (AdvGLUE++ source); StableVicuna-13B (AdvGLUE++ source)
Evaluation Metrics: Toxicity Probability=32.0 (GPT-3.5 REALTOXICITYPROMPTS-Toxic); Toxicity Probability=31.0 (GPT-4 REALTOXICITYPROMPTS-Toxic); Expected Maximum Toxicity (Adversarial Prompt)=0.86 (GPT-3.5 REALTOXICITYPROMPTS-Toxic); Expected Maximum Toxicity (Adversarial Prompt)=0.94 (GPT-4 REALTOXICITYPROMPTS-Toxic) | other metrics: Expected Maximum Toxicity (Perspective API); agreementIndex (stereotype agreement rate); Robust Accuracy on AdvGLUE / AdvGLUE++; Attack Success Rate (ASR); Refusal Rate (RR) and Non-Existence Rate (NE)
Key Results: Adversarial system prompts push GPT-4 toxicity probability from 31% (benign) to 100% on REALTOXICITYPROMPTS, showing alignment is bypassed by jailbreaking system prompts. | AdvGLUE++ adversarial texts cut GPT-4 robust accuracy from 78.18% on AdvGLUE to 55.64% (Alpaca-source), and GPT-3.5 from 67.37% to 49.23%. | 5-shot prompting with known email domain extracts up to 48.19% (GPT-4) and 44.04% (GPT-3.5) of Enron email addresses; unknown-domain rate is ~100x lower. | Combined jailbreaking prompts raise FPR on ETHICS from 4% (benign) to 94% on GPT-4 and to 65.5% on GPT-3.5 (ΔFPR +90% / +59.5%). | Aggregated DecodingTrust scores: Llama-v2-7B-Chat best on Toxicity 80, Bias 97.6, Privacy 97.4, Fairness 100; GPT-4 best on Adv 64.04, OoD 87.55; GPT-3.5 best on Demo 81.28 and ME 86.38.
Strengths: First comprehensive eight-dimension trust benchmark on GPT-3.5/GPT-4 with 270K+ prompts, covering toxicity, bias, robustness, privacy, ethics, and fairness. | Releases a publicly available, extensible toolkit and leaderboard, evaluated on six open LLMs (Llama-2, Vicuna, Alpaca, MPT, Falcon, RedPajama) plus GPT models. | Surfaces a counter-intuitive finding that GPT-4 follows jailbreak instructions more precisely and is therefore more vulnerable than GPT-3.5 under misleading prompts. | Introduces new attack constructions (33 system prompts, AdvGLUE++, evasive sentences, jailbreak ethical prompts) that go well beyond static benchmarks.
Limitations: Pretraining data of GPT-3.5/GPT-4 is closed, so failures cannot be traced to causes and OOD design rests on hypotheses. | Trust dimensions like toxicity and ethics are subjective; the paper provides objective metrics without human-alignment validation. | Snapshot of GPT models on March 2023; conclusions may not hold as APIs evolve. | Released jailbreaking prompts could be misused to fine-tune models against the benchmark itself.

Author: Kirsten
Title: The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs
Contribution: Probes how five inference acceleration strategies (INT4/INT8, AWQ, KV4/KV8, structured/unstructured Wanda pruning) change demographic bias in three instruction-tuned LLMs across six bias metrics.
Dataset: CrowSPairs; GlobalOpinionQA; WorldBench; DT-Stereotyping; DiscrimEval; DiscrimEvalGen
Data Size: 1,508 CrowSPairs prompts; 9,450 DiscrimEval prompts; 70 DiscrimEvalGen scenarios; 2,556 GlobalOpinionQA questions; 2,225 WorldBench questions; 1,152 DT-Stereotyping prompts
Models Used: LLaMA-2-7B-chat; LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3
Evaluation Metrics: Wasserstein-Gini bias=0.16 (Mistral-7B-v0.3 GlobalOpinionQA); Wasserstein-Gini bias=0.15 (Mistral-7B-v0.3 4-bit GlobalOpinionQA); Mean absolute relative error=0.59 (Mistral-7B-v0.3 WorldBench); Bias score=0.49 (LLaMA-2-7B 4-bit DiscrimEval) | other metrics: CrowSPairs stereotype probability score; GlobalOpinionQA Wasserstein-Gini divergence; WorldBench mean absolute relative error; DT-Stereotyping agreement rate; DiscrimEval max-min P(yes) gap
Key Results: AWQ 4-bit on Mistral DiscrimEval rises from 0.21 to 0.94 (+348%) under greedy decoding | Structured Wanda pruning on Mistral DT-Stereotyping drops agreement from 0.87 to 0.26 (-70%) | AWQ on LLaMA-2 WorldBench raises mean error from 0.22 to 0.49 (+123%) | Mistral DT-Stereotyping agreement rate jumps from 34 to 71 under AWQ (+109%)
Strengths: Tests six diverse bias metrics across three modern instruction-tuned LLMs and five acceleration strategies | Introduces a new generation-based bias dataset, DiscrimEvalGen, that forces the model to choose between groups | Releases full code on GitHub for reproducibility of every metric and acceleration setting | Shows that bias effects after quantization are model-specific and direction-unpredictable, contradicting prior uniform claims
Limitations: Benchmark coverage is not exhaustive and may miss domain-specific or harder bias manifestations | Only training-free acceleration is studied; fine-tuning and retraining-based methods are excluded | Fixed hyperparameters (greedy and five-sample nucleus) limit the range of behaviors observed | Results should be read as indicative, not definitive, since bias in modern instruction-tuned LLMs is under-explored

Author: Kwon
Title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
Venue: SOSP '23 (29th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles)
Contribution: Proposes PagedAttention, an attention algorithm that stores KV cache in non-contiguous paged blocks like OS virtual memory, and builds vLLM, a serving system that yields 2-4x throughput over FasterTransformer and Orca.
Dataset: ShareGPT; Alpaca; WMT16 English-to-German translation
Data Size: 1-hour synthetic Poisson traces (15 minutes for OPT-175B); ShareGPT inputs/outputs ~8.4x and ~5.8x longer than Alpaca on average
Models Used: OPT-13B; OPT-66B; OPT-175B; LLaMA-13B
Evaluation Metrics: Throughput speedup over SOTA=2-4x (OPT/LLaMA 16-bit ShareGPT/Alpaca); Effective KV cache memory utilization (%)=20.4-38.2 (OPT-13B 16-bit ShareGPT/Alpaca); Sustainable request rate vs Orca (Oracle)=1.7-2.7x (OPT (13B/66B/175B), LLaMA-13B 16-bit ShareGPT); Sustainable request rate vs FasterTransformer=22.0 (OPT (13B/66B/175B), LLaMA-13B 16-bit ShareGPT) | other metrics: Normalized latency (mean end-to-end latency divided by output length); Sustained request rate (requests per second); Average number of batched requests; KV-cache memory saving from sharing (%); Effective KV-cache memory utilization (%)
Key Results: vLLM yields 2-4x throughput improvement over FasterTransformer and Orca at the same level of latency | On ShareGPT, vLLM sustains 1.7-2.7x higher request rates than Orca (Oracle) and 2.7-8x higher than Orca (Max); up to 22x higher than FasterTransformer | Beam search with width 6 on OPT-13B/Alpaca: improvement over Orca (Oracle) grows from 1.3x (basic sampling) to 2.3x; KV memory savings of 37.6-55.2% | Shared-prefix translation (LLaMA-13B, WMT16): 1.67x throughput over Orca (Oracle) for 1-shot prefix, 3.58x for 5-shot prefix | Existing systems waste ~80% of KV cache memory; only 20.4-38.2% of KV cache stores actual token states
Strengths: Cuts KV cache memory waste from ~80% to near zero, allowing 2-4x more requests per batch on the same GPU. | Enables flexible KV cache sharing across sequences for parallel sampling, beam search, and shared prefixes via copy-on-write. | Open-source code released; widely adopted backbone for LLM serving research and production. | Throughput gains scale with longer sequences, larger models, and more complex decoding algorithms.
Limitations: PagedAttention adds 20-26% overhead to the attention kernel versus the highly-optimised FasterTransformer kernel. | Authors note paging benefits do not generalise: workloads with static shapes or compute-bound serving may see no gain or a slowdown. | Swapping recovery suffers from small-block PCIe overhead; recomputation only matches it for medium block sizes. | Block-size choice is a tradeoff: too small underutilises GPU, too large increases internal fragmentation and reduces sharing.

Author: Hong
Title: Decoding Compressed Trust: Scrutinizing the Trustworthiness of Efficient LLMs Under Compression
Venue: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235)
Contribution: First comprehensive evaluation of compressed LLMs on trustworthiness across eight DecodingTrust dimensions, comparing five SoTA quantization and pruning methods.
Dataset: MMLU; DecodingTrust; AdvGLUE++; C4 (calibration); MT-Bench
Data Size: 128 calibration sequences for GPTQ/AWQ/SparseGPT/Wanda; MMLU 57 tasks; DecodingTrust 33 test cases across 8 trust metrics
Models Used: LLAMA2 13b; LLAMA2 13b Chat; Vicuna 13b Chat; LLAMA2 7b Chat; LLAMA2 70b Chat
Evaluation Metrics: MT-Bench Score (1-10)=2.89 (Llama-2-13B-Chat 3-bit MT-Bench); Ethics Score (text)=76.3 (Llama-2-13B-Chat 4-bit DecodingTrust-Ethics); Trustworthiness drop (worst-case)=50.0 (Llama-2-13B-Chat 3-bit DecodingTrust-Toxicity); Trustworthiness drop=30.0 (Llama-2-13B-Chat 3-bit DecodingTrust-OOD) | other metrics: MMLU accuracy; DecodingTrust 8-dimension trust score (0-100); Refusal rate; False Positive Rate (FPR); Equalized Odds Difference (EOD)
Key Results: LLAMA2 13b Chat at 4-bit GPTQ improves Ethics from 54.1 to 76.3 (+22.2) and at 4-bit AWQ to 62.8 (+8.7) vs FP16 | LLAMA2 13b Chat 4-bit GPTQ MT-Bench drops to 6.55 vs FP16 7.00; 3-bit GPTQ collapses to 2.89 while AWQ 3-bit holds 6.42 | GPTQ 3-bit causes catastrophic trust drops on LLAMA2 13b Chat: ~30 points OOD robustness and ~50 points Toxicity vs dense | Pruning at 50% sparsity (2:4) significantly degrades trustworthiness while 4-bit quantization preserves it
Strengths: First comprehensive trust evaluation of compressed LLMs across 8 dimensions plus benign MMLU | Tests three models and five SoTA compression methods across multiple bit-widths and sparsity rates | Shows quantization can unexpectedly improve fairness and ethics at moderate bit-widths (4-bit) | Reports multi-seed runs for 3-bit and 4-bit quantization giving variance estimates
Limitations: Limited to 13b-class models for main analysis; 7b/70b only briefly tested with GPTQ | Restricted to 2:4 semi-structured pruning, excluding broader unstructured pruning regimes | GPTQ at 3-bit shows large variance (up to 15 points) making the result unpredictable | Authors modify DecodingTrust scoring to handle large refusal-rate biases, complicating cross-paper comparison

Author: Zhelnin
Title: GIFT-SW: Gaussian noise Injected Fine-Tuning of Salient Weights for LLMs
Contribution: GIFT-SW is a PEFT method that updates only salient weight columns while injecting Gaussian noise into non-salient columns; it also recovers performance of mixed-precision quantized LLMs.
Dataset: TULU-V2-Mix; OpenOrca; Pile (validation); WikiText-2; HellaSwag; BoolQ; WinoGrande; PiQA; ARC-easy; ARC-challenge
Data Size: 512 random sentences from the Pile validation set for sensitivity calibration; 128 random Wikitext-2 samples for GPTQ Hessian; 500 training iterations (one epoch, batch 128 for 7B / 64 for 13B)
Models Used: LLaMA2-7B; LLaMA2-13B; LLaMA3-8B; TULU2-7B; TULU2-13B
Evaluation Metrics: Mean accuracy (%)=73.33 (LLaMA2-7b 16-bit TULU-V2-mix); Mean accuracy (%)=75.93 (LLaMA2-13b 16-bit TULU-V2-mix); Mean accuracy (%)=72.53 (LLaMA2-7b 4-bit TULU-V2-mix); Mean accuracy (%)=61.09 (LLaMA2-7b 2-bit TULU-V2-mix) | other metrics: Zero-shot accuracy (mean across 6 benchmarks); Per-benchmark accuracy on BoolQ, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, PiQA
Key Results: GIFT-SW reaches 73.33 mean accuracy on LLaMA2-7B with TULU-V2-mix, beating FT (71.97), LoRA (71.78) and DoRA (72.03) | At 2-bit quantization GIFT-SW reaches 61.09 on LLaMA2-7B vs STE 58.20 and QUIK+LoRA 41.44 (more than 5 points over second-best) | GIFT-SW matches TULU2 on LLaMA2-7B (73.33 vs 73.49) using 174M trainable params and 500 iters vs 6.7B / 5K (~10x less compute) | Pre-GIFT-SW outperforms at 4-bit (73.15 vs 72.53 Post-GIFT-SW) on LLaMA2-7B but Post-GIFT-SW dominates at 2-bit (61.09 vs 47.08)
Strengths: Outperforms full FT, LoRA, and DoRA on LLaMA2-7B/13B and LLaMA3-8B with the same training budget across most zero-shot tasks. | At 2-bit quantization GIFT-SW beats STE and QUIK+LoRA by more than 5 points on average accuracy. | Matches or beats TULU2 on LLaMA2 using ~3% of parameters and roughly ten times less compute. | More stable than LoRA/DoRA across data budgets; performance scales smoothly with training data size.
Limitations: Results reported only on LLaMA models; transfer to other architectures is untested. | Only GPTQ (via QUIK) used for quantization; other PTQ methods like RTN or QuantEase not tested. | No CUDA kernels provided; lacks an efficient implementation of the algorithm for inference. | Authors could not confirm models trained with noise injection are more robust to further degradation (Q3).

Author: Ashkboos
Title: SliceGPT: Compress Large Language Models by Deleting Rows and Columns
Contribution: SliceGPT is a post-training structured pruning method that applies an orthogonal transform (computational invariance) and slices entire rows and columns of weight matrices, reducing the embedding dimension while keeping competitive accuracy without recovery fine-tuning.
Dataset: WikiText-2; Alpaca; PIQA; WinoGrande; HellaSwag; ARC-e; ARC-c
Data Size: Calibration set size 1024 sequences with sequence length 2048 (main experiments); ablations from 128 to 4096
Models Used: OPT-125M; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; LLaMA-2-7B; LLaMA-2-13B; LLaMA-2-70B; Phi-2
Evaluation Metrics: Avg Accuracy retention vs Dense (%)=99 (LLAMA-2 70B Zero-shot avg (PIQA/WinoGrande/HellaSwag/ARC-e/ARC-c)); Avg Accuracy retention vs Dense (%)=99 (OPT 66B Zero-shot avg (PIQA/WinoGrande/HellaSwag/ARC-e/ARC-c)); Avg Accuracy retention vs Dense (%)=90 (Phi-2 Zero-shot avg (PIQA/WinoGrande/HellaSwag/ARC-e/ARC-c)); Total compute relative to dense (%)=64 (LLAMA-2 70B RTX6000 24GB) | other metrics: WikiText-2 perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy (PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c, average); Per-token inference time (ms) and total compute (GPUms); Throughput (tokens/sec)
Key Results: LLaMA-2 70B sliced 25% reaches WikiText-2 PPL 4.60 vs dense 3.32 (Δ 1.28); SparseGPT 2:4 reaches 4.98 | Sliced models keep 99% (LLAMA-2 70B), 99% (OPT 66B) and 90% (Phi-2) of zero-shot accuracy at 25% slicing (90% Phi-2 with RFT) | LLaMA-2 70B at 25% slicing: 110ms/token on 3 A100s vs 125ms on 4 (compute reduced to 66%); 215ms on 5 RTX6000 vs 252ms on 7 (reduced to 64%) | LLaMA-2 70B sliced 25% achieves 1.55x throughput on 80GB H100 (839 vs 541 tokens/s); 50% achieves 3.75x on a single GPU
Strengths: Structured sliced models use dense kernels and run faster on standard hardware without custom sparse code. | Reduces inference compute on LLaMA-2 70B to 64% on RTX6000 and 66% on A100, cutting GPU count. | Single-shot method: no recovery fine-tuning needed to keep most accuracy at 25% slicing. | Beats SparseGPT 2:4 in WikiText-2 PPL on every LLaMA-2 size at 25% slicing.
Limitations: Sliced LLaMA-2 models lose more accuracy than OPT models because LLaMA-2's eigenvalue spectrum is flatter. | Smaller models (under 13B) gain less from slicing because they hold less spare embedding dimension. | Adds a small DxD residual-connection overhead per block that cannot be pre-computed. | Sliced models keep more parameters than SparseGPT 2:4 at matched compute, since slicing does not exploit unstructured zeros.

Author: Ashkboos
Title: QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs
Contribution: QuaRot is a rotation-based PTQ scheme that fuses randomized Hadamard transforms into LLM weights to eliminate activation outliers, enabling end-to-end 4-bit quantization of weights, activations, and KV cache with minimal accuracy loss.
Dataset: WikiText-2; PIQA; WinoGrande; HellaSwag; LAMBADA (OpenAI); ARC-Easy; ARC-Challenge
Data Size: 128 samples of 2048-token sequences from WikiText-2 training set used as the GPTQ calibration set
Models Used: LLaMA-2-7B; LLaMA-2-13B; LLaMA-2-70B; LLaMA-3-8B; LLaMA-3-70B; Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity=6.1 (LLAMA2-7B 4-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=3.79 (LLAMA2-70B 4-bit WikiText-2); Average Accuracy=75.98 (LLAMA2-70B 4-bit Zero-shot Avg (6 tasks)); Prefill Speedup over FP16=2.16 (LLAMA2-7B 4-bit RTX 3090 (batch=64)) | other metrics: WikiText-2 perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy (PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, ARC-E, ARC-C, LAMBADA, average); Peak memory saving during decoding; Per-layer runtime (ms) on RTX 3090
Key Results: LLaMA-2-70B 4-bit (W4A4KV4) QuaRot reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.79 vs FP16 3.32 (delta 0.47), beating QUIK-4B (6.91) with 0 outlier features | LLaMA-2-70B at 4-bit QuaRot retains 75.98% zero-shot average vs 77.07% FP16 (1.09% drop, ~99% retention) | Up to 3.33x prefill speedup on LLaMA-2-70B and 2.16x on LLaMA-2-7B over FP16 on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 | Decoding-stage peak memory saving up to 3.89x on LLaMA-2-70B and 3.75x on LLaMA-2-7B over FP16
Strengths: First end-to-end 4-bit scheme that quantizes weights, activations, and KV cache without keeping outlier channels in higher precision. | Strong accuracy retention: LLaMA-2-70B at 4-bit loses at most 0.47 PPL on WikiText-2 and keeps 99% of zero-shot accuracy. | Real consumer-GPU speedups: up to 3.33x prefill speedup on LLaMA-2-70B and up to 3.89x decoding memory saving on RTX 3090. | Lossless 6- and 8-bit quantization without any calibration data, using simple round-to-nearest weight quantization.
Limitations: 4-bit RTN weight quantization shows a large gap to GPTQ on small models (LLaMA-2-7B PPL rises from 6.10 to 8.37). | 4-bit KV cache offers no decoding speedup at small batch sizes (<=8); benefit only appears at large batch or long sequence. | LLaMA-3 is more sensitive to 4-bit quantization than LLaMA-2, with larger PPL gaps to FP16 (8.16 vs 6.14 on LLaMA-3-8B). | Performance results measured on a single transformer block since the full model does not fit on the GPU cluster used.

Author: Egiazarian
Title: Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization
Contribution: AQLM extends classic Additive Quantization (a multi-codebook method from information retrieval) to LLM weight compression, achieving Pareto-optimal accuracy below 3 bits per parameter and strong results in the 2-bit regime, with practical GPU/CPU kernels.
Dataset: WikiText-2; C4; WinoGrande; PiQA; HellaSwag; ARC-easy; ARC-challenge; RedPajama (calibration)
Data Size: Calibration uses RedPajama subset at 4096-token sequences (8M tokens for LLAMA 2; 4M for QuIP). End-to-end fine-tuning uses 4-16M training tokens.
Models Used: LLAMA 2 7B; LLAMA 2 13B; LLAMA 2 70B; Mixtral 8x7B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity=4.94 (LLAMA-2-13B 2-bit WikiText-2); Perplexity=3.94 (LLAMA-2-70B 2-bit WikiText-2); Average Zero-shot Accuracy=68.75 (LLAMA-2-70B 2-bit WinoGrande+PiQA+HellaSwag+ArcE+ArcC); Speedup over FP16 (gate_proj matvec)=3.05 (LLAMA-2-70B 2-bit RTX 3090 GPU) | other metrics: Perplexity (WikiText-2); Perplexity (C4); Zero-shot accuracy (5 tasks averaged); Average bits per parameter; Matrix-vector multiplication latency (microseconds)
Key Results: LLAMA 2 70B at 2.07-bit AQLM reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.94 vs FP16 3.12, beating QuIP# 2.01-bit (PPL 4.16) and average zero-shot accuracy 68.75 vs 67.67 | LLAMA 2 7B at 2.02-bit AQLM gets WikiText-2 PPL 6.59 vs QuIP# 8.22 at the same bit budget (FP16 baseline 5.12) | LLAMA 2 70B at 3.01-bit AQLM reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.36 vs FP16 3.12, beating GPTQ 4.40 and QuIP 3.87 at 3 bits | GPU matrix-vector speedup of x1.20-x1.31 over FP16 on RTX 3090; CPU 2x8-bit AQLM gives up to x4.07 speedup over FP32 on Intel i9 for LLAMA 2 70B
Strengths: First scheme to be Pareto optimal below 3 bits per parameter, beating QuIP# and prior baselines across LLAMA 2 7B/13B/70B at 2-3 bit budgets. | Provides fast GPU and CPU kernels that match or beat FP16 latency, with up to x4 CPU speedup and around 14 tokens/s on LLAMA 2 70B. | Uses a homogeneous quantized format with no sparse outlier matrix, making it simpler to deploy than mixed sparse-quantized methods like SpQR. | Open-source GitHub release of code and quantized checkpoints supports reproducibility.
Limitations: More compute-expensive than direct PTQ methods like RTN or GPTQ because of the more complex coding representation. | Strict 2-bit AQLM is not Pareto optimal for the same model; only the 2.5-bit point becomes Pareto optimal. | Beam search picked for codes is not the fastest MRF solver; randomized ICM could be faster but was not implemented. | Codebook update uses Adam as a workaround instead of a closed-form least-squares solver, leaving extra hyperparameters in the loop.

Author: Zhang
Title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
Contribution: H2O is a KV cache eviction policy that dynamically retains a balance of recent and Heavy-Hitter tokens, reducing KV cache memory while preserving accuracy and improving generation throughput up to 29x over leading inference systems.
Dataset: Wiki-Text-103; COPA; MathQA; OpenBookQA; PiQA; RTE; Winogrande; XSUM; CNN/Daily Mail; AlpacaEval; MT-bench; PG-19; Penn Treebank; Amazon Review
Data Size: 1000 test samples for HELM tasks (XSUM, CNN/Daily Mail); 5-shot evaluation for lm-eval-harness tasks; synthetic prompts of various lengths (512, 2048, 7000) for throughput tests
Models Used: OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; OPT-175B; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; GPT-NeoX-20B; GPT-2
Evaluation Metrics: Throughput speedup over FlexGen=3.0 (OPT-6.7B 16-bit Synthetic 512+32); Throughput speedup over DeepSpeed=29.0 (OPT-6.7B 16-bit Synthetic 512+32); Throughput speedup over Accelerate=29.0 (OPT-6.7B 16-bit Synthetic 512+32); Latency reduction vs FlexGen=1.9 (OPT-6.7B 16-bit Synthetic) | other metrics: Accuracy on downstream tasks; Generation throughput (token/s); Latency (seconds); Perplexity (PPL); Self-BLEU diversity
